policy: Concise audible recognition cues, written individually for each concept as continuations of “Listen For”; start each cue lowercase and end only the final cue with a full stop. Never copy sentences from the main definition.

MC-0001.name: Blues
cues: four beats per bar and a recurring 12-bar chord cycle
flattened notes, bent pitches and answering phrases
riffs and improvised solos.

MC-0002.name: Jazz
cues: syncopated rhythms, often with a swung feel
improvised solos, often on saxophone, trumpet or piano.

MC-0003.name: Latin American
cues: lively dance pulse with off-beat rhythms
prominent bongos, claves, shakers or a scraping güiro.

MC-0004.name: Musical
cues: theatrical solo or group singing with a band or orchestra
a direct, popular-style vocal delivery with clear words
spoken dialogue alternating with songs.

MC-0005.name: Pop
cues: lead vocals with guitar, keyboards, bass and a regular drum beat
catchy choruses, repeated hooks and returning verse tunes.

MC-0006.name: Rock
cues: heavy, driving drum beat
distorted guitar riffs with bass and vocals.

MC-0007.name: Rock 'n' roll
cues: fast, lively backbeat with repeated riffs
a walking bass and 12-bar blues pattern.

MC-0008.name: Scottish
cues: fiddle, accordion or droning bagpipes, often with a strong dance pulse
songs using Scots or Gaelic words.

MC-0009.name: Ascending
cues: the notes climbing higher.

MC-0010.name: Chord
cues: several pitches sounding as one block.

MC-0011.name: Chord change
cues: a shift in the accompanying chord sound.

MC-0012.name: Descending
cues: the notes moving lower.

MC-0013.name: Discord
cues: clashing pitches that sound tense or unsettled.

MC-0014.name: Improvisation
cues: free, spontaneous-sounding phrases, often varying a familiar tune or backing pattern.

MC-0015.name: Leap / leaping
cues: the tune making noticeable pitch jumps, skipping neighbouring scale notes.

MC-0016.name: Question and answer
cues: a short phrase followed by a balancing reply
similar rhythms or phrase lengths.

MC-0017.name: Repetition
cues: the same musical idea coming back unchanged.

MC-0018.name: Sequence
cues: the same part immediately restating a phrase higher or lower
a recognisable rhythm and melodic shape in each restatement.

MC-0019.name: Step / stepwise
cues: the tune moving up or down through neighbouring scale notes.

MC-0020.name: 2, 3 or 4 beats in the bar
cues: a recurring strong beat followed by weaker beats
the pulse falling into groups of two, three or four.

MC-0021.name: Accent / accented
cues: one note standing out with extra force.

MC-0022.name: Adagio
cues: a slow, unhurried pace.

MC-0023.name: Allegro
cues: a quick, lively pace.

MC-0024.name: Beat / pulse
cues: a regular pulse you can tap along to.

MC-0025.name: Drum fill
cues: a brief burst of extra drum notes
a drum fill leading into a new phrase or section.

MC-0026.name: Faster
cues: the pulse becoming quicker.

MC-0027.name: March
cues: firm, even beats at a walking pace
clear groups of two or four, often with strong percussion.

MC-0028.name: Off the beat
cues: emphasis between main beats or on weaker beats, such as 2 and 4.

MC-0029.name: On the beat
cues: notes landing with the main pulse
reinforced strong beats, such as 1 and 3.

MC-0030.name: Pause
cues: a note or silence lasting longer than expected.

MC-0031.name: Reel
cues: fast, flowing Scottish dance rhythm
two or four beats, dividing evenly into twos.

MC-0032.name: Slower
cues: the pulse becoming less quick.

MC-0033.name: Waltz
cues: a repeating ONE-two-three dance pulse
a bass note followed by two lighter chords.

MC-0034.name: Accompanied
cues: supporting music underneath the main tune.

MC-0035.name: Harmony / chord
cues: different pitches sounding together in chords or separate voice parts.

MC-0037.name: Ostinato / riff
cues: a short tune or rhythm looping repeatedly.

MC-0038.name: Round
cues: the same tune starting at different times in overlapping parts
each part looping back to the beginning.

MC-0039.name: Solo
cues: one featured singer or instrument standing out.

MC-0040.name: Unaccompanied
cues: the main voice or instrument sounding without backing.

MC-0041.name: Unison / octave
cues: several performers sharing one tune at the same pitch.

MC-0042.name: Accordion
cues: a bright, reedy, sustained tone
a melody over alternating bass notes and chords.

MC-0043.name: Acoustic guitar
cues: clear, resonant strums or individually plucked notes
notes ringing briefly, then fading.

MC-0044.name: Bagpipes
cues: a piercing, ornamented tune over continuous low drones.

MC-0045.name: Blowing
cues: airy, reedy or brassy tones, sometimes with audible breaths.

MC-0046.name: Bowing
cues: a sustained string tone, often smoothly joined between notes.

MC-0047.name: Brass
cues: a bright, brassy or mellow rounded tone
powerful fanfares, sustained chords or bold melodies.

MC-0048.name: Choir
cues: many voices blending in unison or harmony.

MC-0049.name: Drum kit
cues: a repeating groove combining deep thuds, snare rattles and cymbal sounds.

MC-0050.name: Electric guitar
cues: amplified guitar notes or chords, sometimes sustained or distorted.

MC-0051.name: Fiddle
cues: a bright bowed violin sound in a folk tune
quick ornaments and dance rhythms.

MC-0052.name: Folk group
cues: a small acoustic group, with or without singing
a blend of acoustic guitar, fiddle, whistle, accordion or bagpipes.

MC-0053.name: Legato
cues: smoothly joined notes with no obvious breaks.

MC-0054.name: Orchestra
cues: a large instrumental sound blending strings, winds, brass and percussion.

MC-0055.name: Organ
cues: long-held keyboard tones that do not quickly die away
full chords and deep pedal notes.

MC-0056.name: Percussion (tuned and untuned)
cues: a mix of definite pitches and untuned rhythmic sounds
struck, shaken or scraped attacks.

MC-0057.name: Piano
cues: a clear struck attack followed by a fading ring
a melody and chords heard together
sharp contrasts between soft and loud notes.

MC-0058.name: Plucking
cues: a sharp string attack followed by a quick fade.

MC-0059.name: Scottish dance band
cues: dance tunes from Scotland led by accordion or fiddle
a steady piano, bass and drum backing.

MC-0060.name: Staccato
cues: clipped notes with audible spaces between them.

MC-0061.name: Steel band
cues: bright, metallic, bell-like pan tones
melody, chords and bass played by different pans.

MC-0062.name: Striking / hitting
cues: a clear impact or hit at the start of each sound.

MC-0063.name: Strings
cues: blending bowed tones or short plucked attacks
high violin lines through to deep bass notes.

MC-0064.name: Strumming
cues: a sweeping chord sound as several strings ring together.

MC-0067.name: Voice
cues: human singing or speech, with recognisable words, vowels or breaths.

MC-0068.name: Woodwind
cues: airy, whistling or reedy tones in the instrumental lines.

MC-0069.name: African music
cues: layered drum patterns and interlocking rhythms
repeated ideas, call and response, voices or clapping.

MC-0070.name: Baroque
cues: interweaving parts, ornaments and repeated sequences
continuous bass-and-chord support, often with harpsichord or organ

MC-0071.name: Concerto
cues: one solo instrument trading phrases with the orchestra

MC-0072.name: Mouth music
cues: rapid Gaelic or nonsense syllables fitting a dance rhythm

MC-0073.name: Opera
cues: operatic solo voices or chorus with orchestral backing

MC-0074.name: Ragtime
cues: syncopated piano tune over a steady bass-note–chord pattern.

MC-0075.name: Rapping
cues: rhythmic, rhyming speech over a backing beat.

MC-0076.name: Reggae
cues: clipped guitar or piano chords emphasising off-beats, often beats 2 and 4

MC-0077.name: Romantic
cues: long, sweeping melodies with expressive give-and-take in tempo

a full, colourful orchestral sound.

MC-0078.name: Scots ballad
cues: a story sung in Scots

one singer with sparse backing or no instruments.

MC-0079.name: Swing
cues: uneven long-short pairs of notes

MC-0080.name: Broken chord / arpeggio

MC-0081.name: Change of key

MC-0082.name: Chord progressions — chords I, IV and V (major keys)

MC-0083.name: Drone
cues: a held or repeated low note/open fifth beneath a moving tune.

MC-0084.name: Major
cues: a bright, happy or cheerful character.

MC-0085.name: Minor
cues: a darker, sadder or more serious character.

MC-0086.name: Octave
cues: two matching note sounds, eight scale notes apart.

MC-0087.name: Ornament
cues: quick decorative notes around the main tune.

MC-0088.name: Pedal
cues: a held or repeating bass note underneath changing chords

MC-0089.name: Pentatonic scale
cues: a tune built from five pitches
an open, folk-like sound without semitone steps.

MC-0090.name: Scale
cues: a run of neighbouring notes climbing or falling in order.

MC-0091.name: Scat singing
cues: improvised vocal runs on “doo”, “ba” or other wordless syllables

MC-0093.name: Vamp

MC-0094.name: A tempo
cues: the earlier speed returning after a temporary change.

MC-0095.name: Accelerando
cues: the pulse speeding up little by little.

MC-0096.name: Anacrusis
cues: pickup notes leading into the first strong beat.

MC-0097.name: Andante
cues: a calm, walking-speed pulse.

MC-0098.name: Compound time
cues: a rolling three-part subdivision of each main beat

MC-0099.name: Dotted rhythms
cues: unequal long-short or short-long note pairs.

MC-0100.name: Jig
cues: a quick, lilting Scottish or Irish dance
two main beats, each dividing into three.

MC-0101.name: Rallentando
cues: the pulse easing back gradually.

MC-0102.name: Scotch snap
cues: a sharply accented short note followed by a longer one.

MC-0103.name: Simple time (2/4, 3/4 and 4/4)

MC-0104.name: Strathspey

dotted rhythms and clipped short-long Scotch snaps.

MC-0105.name: Syncopation
cues: accents landing off the strong beats, or notes carrying across them.

MC-0106.name: Cadenza
cues: a showy solo passage, usually with little or no backing

MC-0107.name: Canon
cues: one tune copied exactly by a later-entering part
the overlapping lines continuing together.

MC-0108.name: Imitation
cues: one part copying a recognisable idea just heard in another.

MC-0109.name: Middle 8
cues: a contrasting passage interrupting the familiar verse or chorus
a passage lasting about eight bars.

MC-0110.name: Ternary / ABA
cues: opening music, contrasting middle, then the opening music again.

MC-0111.name: Theme and variation
cues: a recognisable tune returning with changed rhythm, decoration, instruments or accompaniment.

MC-0112.name: Verse and chorus
cues: the verse melody repeating with new words
a contrasting chorus returning with familiar words and music.

MC-0113.name: Alto
cues: a low female singing line, beneath soprano.

MC-0114.name: Backing vocals
cues: extra voices behind the lead singer
harmonies, echoes or held backing notes.

MC-0115.name: Bass
cues: the deepest adult male singing line.

MC-0116.name: Bass drum
cues: a deep, low thump beneath the other percussion.

MC-0117.name: Bass guitar
cues: a low, amplified, plucked line supporting the groove.

MC-0118.name: Brass band
cues: a full blend of brass with percussion
an ensemble sound without bowed strings or woodwind lines.

MC-0119.name: Cello
cues: a warm, singing string tone, lower than violin but higher than double bass

MC-0120.name: Clarinet
cues: a rounded, reedy tone
darker low notes and clear, bright high notes.

MC-0121.name: Cymbals
cues: metallic crashes or a lingering shimmer.

MC-0122.name: Distortion
cues: a rough, fuzzy or gritty amplified tone.

MC-0123.name: Double bass
cues: very deep string notes
bowed rumble or a plucked, resonant bass line.

MC-0124.name: Flute
cues: a clear, airy high tone
light, flowing runs or a breathy melody.

MC-0125.name: Glockenspiel

MC-0126.name: Guiro

MC-0127.name: Harp
cues: resonant plucked notes, rippling chords or sweeping glissandi.

MC-0128.name: Harpsichord

MC-0129.name: Muted

MC-0130.name: Pan pipes
cues: a breathy, hollow whistle changing between pitches.

MC-0131.name: Recorder
cues: a clear, whistle-like tone, often with an airy edge.

MC-0132.name: Saxophone
cues: a strong, reedy tone, often breathy or slightly husky
a saxophone line in jazz solos or big bands.

MC-0133.name: Snare drum
cues: a sharp, rattling drum sound
rapid rolls creating a continuous buzz.

MC-0134.name: Soprano
cues: the highest adult female singing line.

MC-0135.name: Tambourine
cues: bright jingles, sometimes mixed with a hand-drum tap.

MC-0136.name: Tenor
cues: a high adult male singing line.

MC-0137.name: Timpani
cues: deep, rounded drum notes with a recognisable pitch
rolls creating a sustained rumble.

MC-0138.name: Triangle
cues: a high, clear metallic ping that rings on.

MC-0139.name: Trombone
cues: a bold, low-to-middle brass tone
audible slides between pitches.

MC-0140.name: Trumpet
cues: a bright, ringing high brass sound, often clear and piercing.

MC-0141.name: Violin
cues: a bright, high bowed-string line
short, lightly plucked notes.

MC-0142.name: Wind band
cues: a blend of woodwind, brass and percussion
an ensemble sound without the bowed strings of an orchestra.

MC-0143.name: Xylophone
cues: hard, bright wooden knocks with clear pitches and a short decay.

MC-0144.name: Aria
cues: a tuneful operatic solo over orchestral backing
shaped, lyrical phrases, often with sustained notes and vibrato.

MC-0145.name: Bothy ballad
cues: a male soloist telling a rural-life story in Scots dialect
unaccompanied singing, with others sometimes joining the chorus
the same tune returning through many verses.

MC-0146.name: Celtic rock
cues: traditional sounds such as fiddle or bagpipes over electric guitar, bass and drums.

MC-0147.name: Chorus
cues: a large body of singers sharing each voice part
several choral lines with orchestral backing.

MC-0148.name: Classical
cues: clear tunes and balanced question-and-answer phrases
mostly melody with accompaniment
light, orderly textures, sometimes with Alberti bass.

MC-0149.name: Gaelic psalm
cues: unaccompanied Gaelic congregation singing
a leader starting each line, followed by the group
slow, ornamented voices overlapping unevenly.

MC-0150.name: Gospel
cues: expressive lead singing answered by a group
strong rhythmic backing, often with clapping
religious words and improvised vocal decoration.

MC-0151.name: Indian

tabla drums repeating a rhythmic cycle
freely improvised, ornamented melodic lines.

MC-0152.name: Minimalist

MC-0153.name: Pibroch

a theme returning with increasingly elaborate grace-note decoration.

MC-0154.name: Symphony
cues: a full orchestra with changing instrumental colours
contrasting themes or movements within a large-scale work.

MC-0155.name: Waulking song
cues: rhythmic Gaelic singing, usually by women without instruments
a solo line answered by the group
a steady thudding or tapping pulse beneath the voices.

MC-0156.name: Atonal
cues: the absence of a clear home note or major/minor key
unsettled, clashing harmony.

MC-0157.name: Chord progressions - chords I, IV, V and VI in a major key
cues: familiar major-key chord changes
major-sounding chords I, IV and V, with VI introducing a minor colour.

MC-0158.name: Chromatic
cues: a line creeping up or down in semitone steps.

MC-0159.name: Cluster
cues: a dense block of tightly clashing neighbouring pitches.

MC-0160.name: Contrary motion
cues: one line climbing while another falls.

MC-0161.name: Countermelody
cues: a distinct secondary tune heard at the same time as the main melody.

MC-0162.name: Descant (voice)
cues: an extra vocal tune above the main singing line
the extra line entering on a later verse and making the texture brighter.

MC-0163.name: Glissando
cues: a smooth pitch slide, or a rapid keyboard/harp sweep.

MC-0164.name: Grace note
cues: a tiny, quick flick just before a main note.

MC-0165.name: Imperfect cadence
cues: a phrase stopping on the dominant chord
an open ending, as though more music should follow.

MC-0166.name: Inverted pedal
cues: a held or repeating high note above moving lower chords.

MC-0167.name: Melismatic
cues: one syllable stretching across several changing pitches.

MC-0168.name: Modulation
cues: a new home key becoming established during the music.

MC-0169.name: Perfect cadence
cues: chord V moving to I at a phrase ending
a strong, settled full-stop effect.

MC-0170.name: Pitch bend
cues: a held note bending smoothly up or down.

MC-0171.name: Semitone
cues: a very small pitch step: the gap to the nearest standard note.

MC-0172.name: Syllabic
cues: a separate note for each syllable, making the words clear.

MC-0173.name: Tone
cues: a whole-step gap, twice the size of a semitone.

MC-0174.name: Trill
cues: a rapid shake between a note and its upper neighbour.

MC-0175.name: Whole-tone scale
cues: six equally spaced pitches, with no small semitone gaps
a floating sound without a strong pull home.

MC-0176.name: Compound time (6/8, 9/8 and 12/8)
cues: each strong pulse dividing into three quavers
two main beats in 6/8, three in 9/8 or four in 12/8.

MC-0177.name: Cross rhythms
cues: competing accents or rhythmic groupings heard at the same time
a two-against-three effect, or 3+3+2 over a four-beat pulse.

MC-0178.name: Moderato
cues: a medium pace: neither quick nor slow.

MC-0179.name: Ritardando
cues: a gradual easing of the speed.

MC-0180.name: Rubato
cues: expressive pushing forward and holding back of the tempo.

MC-0181.name: Alberti bass

this pattern beneath a piano melody.

MC-0182.name: Binary / AB
cues: two different sections, A then B
either section being heard twice.

MC-0183.name: Coda
cues: an extra closing passage rounding off the piece.

MC-0184.name: Contrapuntal
cues: several independent tunes weaving together.

MC-0186.name: Ground bass
cues: the same bass tune returning under changing upper parts.

MC-0187.name: Homophonic
cues: one clear tune with supporting chords
several parts moving together in matching rhythms.

MC-0188.name: Polyphonic
cues: two or more distinct tunes sounding together, each with its own rhythm.

MC-0189.name: Rondo/ABACA — episode
cues: the main tune returning between contrasting sections: A–B–A–C–A
the returning A section in its original key.
the contrasting B and C sections, called episodes, between returns of A.

MC-0190.name: Strophic
cues: the verse tune staying the same while the words change.

MC-0191.name: Walking bass
cues: a moving bass note on every beat
a plucked double bass in jazz.

MC-0192.name: A cappella
cues: voices only, without instrumental backing.

MC-0193.name: Arco
cues: smooth, sustained string tones from the bow.

MC-0194.name: Baritone
cues: a male voice between the high tenor and low bass.

MC-0195.name: Bassoon
cues: a low, woody, reedy tone
a rounded bass line or a nasal-sounding solo.

MC-0196.name: Bodhran
cues: a hollow drum pulse with quick strokes and bending, changing tones.

MC-0197.name: Bongo drums
cues: quick, high hand-drum taps alternating between two pitches.

MC-0198.name: Castanets

MC-0199.name: Clarsach
cues: light, ringing plucked notes, often in a Scottish folk tune.

MC-0200.name: Con sordino
cues: a softened or altered instrumental colour, often veiled or nasal.

MC-0201.name: Flutter-tonguing

MC-0202.name: French horn
cues: warm, mellow brass in a middle register.

MC-0203.name: Hi-hat cymbals
cues: a short metallic “chick” when closed
a longer sizzling sound when open.

MC-0204.name: Mezzo-soprano
cues: a female voice between the high soprano and low alto.

MC-0205.name: Oboe
cues: a focused, penetrating nasal tone in a high woodwind line.

MC-0206.name: Piccolo
cues: an exceptionally high, piercing flute-like sound.

MC-0207.name: Pizzicato
cues: short, lightly plucked string notes that fade quickly.

MC-0208.name: Reverb
cues: a lingering, spacious tail after notes or voices stop
reflections blending together instead of repeating as separate echoes.

MC-0209.name: Rolls
cues: rapid percussion strokes merging into a continuous roll.

MC-0210.name: Sitar
cues: a bright, buzzing plucked melody with ringing resonance
sliding ornaments over a drone.

MC-0211.name: Tabla
cues: two contrasting hand-drum tones in intricate repeating patterns
tabla accompaniment beneath a sitar melody.

MC-0212.name: Tuba
cues: a very deep, rounded brass bass line.

MC-0213.name: Viola
cues: a darker, lower bowed-string tone than violin
an inner harmony line.

MC-0214.name: Chamber music
cues: a small ensemble, with one player carrying each line
exposed instrumental parts exchanging and answering musical ideas.

MC-0215.name: Impressionist
cues: floating whole-tone or modal melodies
parallel chords and unresolved harmonies
a blurred pulse with delicate orchestral colours or ringing piano resonance.

MC-0216.name: Jazz funk
cues: repeated, syncopated bass riffs locked to a strong drum groove
improvised solos with electric keyboard, guitar or synthesiser sounds.

MC-0217.name: Lied
cues: one singer with an expressive piano part
words in German, with voice and piano sharing the musical interest
the piano echoing the words’ mood or action.

MC-0218.name: Mass
cues: words such as “Gloria”, “Credo”, “Sanctus”, “Agnus Dei” or “Kyrie”
interweaving choral lines
instrumental backing or voices alone.

MC-0219.name: Musique concrète
cues: recorded everyday sounds used as musical material

MC-0220.name: Oratorio

MC-0221.name: Plainchant

MC-0222.name: Recitative
cues: solo singing that sounds like heightened speech

MC-0223.name: Sonata
cues: a solo instrument, or an instrument with piano

MC-0224.name: Soul music
cues: passionate, gospel-like lead singing

MC-0225.name: String quartet
cues: four solo strings: two violins, viola and cello

MC-0226.name: Acciaccatura
cues: a very quick crushed note flicking into the main pitch.

MC-0227.name: Added 6th
cues: an extra sixth adding a mellow, jazzy colour to a triad

MC-0228.name: Diminished 7th

MC-0229.name: Diminished triad
cues: a minor-sounding triad with a flattened fifth

MC-0230.name: Dominant 7th

MC-0231.name: Harmonic minor scale

MC-0232.name: Interrupted cadence

MC-0233.name: Interval
cues: the pitch gap between two notes, heard together or one after another.

MC-0234.name: Melodic minor scale
cues: a smoother minor-scale rise with raised sixth and seventh

MC-0235.name: Mode or modal

MC-0236.name: Mordent

MC-0237.name: Obbligato

MC-0238.name: Plagal cadence

MC-0239.name: Relative major

MC-0240.name: Relative minor

MC-0241.name: Tierce de Picardie

MC-0242.name: 3 against 2
cues: one part playing three evenly spaced notes against another part’s two
both groups covering the same time span.

MC-0243.name: Augmentation
cues: a familiar tune returning in longer note values, often twice as long
the accompanying pulse staying steady.

MC-0244.name: Diminution
cues: a familiar tune returning in shorter note values, often half as long
the accompanying pulse staying steady.

MC-0245.name: Irregular time signatures
cues: uneven recurring groups of five or seven, such as 3+2 or 2+2+3.

MC-0246.name: Time changes
cues: changes in the number or grouping of beats during the piece
accents regrouping while the underlying note speed stays the same.

MC-0247.name: Triplets
cues: three equally spaced notes fitted where two would normally go.

MC-0248.name: Basso continuo
cues: a continuous low line with chords above it
harpsichord, organ or lute chords over a cello/bassoon-like bass line.

MC-0249.name: Concerto grosso
cues: a few soloists (concertino) answering a fuller ensemble (ripieno)
low bass and keyboard chords supporting both groups.

MC-0250.name: Da capo aria
cues: an operatic solo in A–B–A form
extra vocal ornaments in the returning A section.

MC-0251.name: Exposition
cues: two contrasting themes, usually in different related keys, in sonata form
the same theme entering in successive parts in a fugue.

MC-0252.name: Passacaglia
cues: a repeating bass foundation with varied music unfolding above it.

MC-0253.name: Ritornello
cues: a recognisable ensemble refrain returning between solo episodes
shortened returns or returns in a new key.

MC-0254.name: Sonata form
cues: two themes in related keys, an exploratory middle, then their return
both themes coming back in the home key.

MC-0255.name: Subject
cues: a distinctive main tune that returns or is developed.

MC-0256.name: Through-composed
cues: new music following the words instead of repeating a verse tune.

MC-0257.name: Coloratura
cues: fast, agile vocal runs, leaps and ornaments
many changing notes on one syllable
a high soprano voice.

MC-0258.name: Concertino
cues: a light group of soloists answering the full ensemble.

MC-0259.name: Harmonics
cues: unusually high, thin or eerie string tones
guitar or harp harmonics ringing like small bells.

MC-0260.name: Ripieno
cues: a fuller, weightier sound when the main ensemble joins in.

MC-0261.name: Tremolando
cues: agitated, trembling strings from rapid repetitions of one pitch
a fast alternation between separated pitches, wider than a trill.

MC-0262.name: Anthem
cues: sacred words in English sung by a choir, sometimes alternating with soloists
organ backing or a cappella passages.

MC-0263.name: Ayre / air
cues: a solo voice, usually with plucked lute accompaniment
a melancholy or reflective character.

MC-0264.name: Ballett
cues: light, dance-like group singing
the tune repeating by verse, ending with “fa-la-la”.

MC-0265.name: Chorale
cues: a hymn tune in four blended voice parts
mostly chordal movement in a clear, regular rhythm
words in German in sung versions.

MC-0266.name: Contemporary jazz
cues: improvised solos over repeating two- or three-chord grooves
complex cross-rhythms, changing metres and chromatic harmony
electronic sounds or unusual instrumental techniques.

MC-0267.name: Electronic dance music (EDM)
cues: a strong programmed dance beat
repeated electronic loops, synth sounds and samples
layered build-ups followed by drops.

MC-0268.name: Galliard
cues: a quick, lively dance pulse in three
closing accents regrouping the beat into twos.

MC-0269.name: Madrigal
cues: non-religious words in English with unaccompanied voices
imitative entries and interweaving parts
word painting and changing music rather than a repeating verse tune.

MC-0270.name: Motet
cues: sacred Latin singing, usually without instruments
flowing choral lines entering imitatively and overlapping.

MC-0271.name: Nationalist
cues: folk-like tunes, dance rhythms or instrumental colours within an art-music setting.

MC-0272.name: Neoclassical
cues: clear, balanced phrases and lean instrumental textures
sharper dissonances or unexpected rhythms within an orderly form.

MC-0273.name: Pavan
cues: a slow, stately dance pulse in two
lute, keyboard or a small early-instrument ensemble.

MC-0274.name: Renaissance
cues: flowing modal melodies and imitative vocal lines
unaccompanied choir, or soft consort colours such as viols and recorders.

MC-0275.name: Serial
cues: angular, often dissonant lines without a clear home key
a twelve-pitch row returning transposed, reversed or mirrored.

MC-0276.name: Appoggiatura
cues: a stressed note on the beat clashing, then stepping to a settled pitch
the stressed note taking noticeable time from the following note.

MC-0277.name: Augmented triad
cues: a major-like chord with a raised fifth
bright but unsettled, with two equal major-third gaps.

MC-0278.name: Chord II and its first inversion (major keys only)
cues: a minor chord on the second scale note, often approaching V
the chord’s third sounding as the lowest note in first inversion.

MC-0279.name: Chords I, IV, V and VI in major and minor keys
cues: major-sounding chords I, IV and V, with a minor VI, in a major key
minor-sounding chords I and IV, with major V and VI, in a minor key.

MC-0280.name: Polytonality / bitonality
cues: two or more different key colours sounding at once
individually tuneful parts clashing when combined.

MC-0281.name: Suspension
cues: a held note clashing as the chord underneath changes
the held note then stepping, usually downwards, into a settled harmony.

MC-0282.name: Tone row / note row
cues: a twelve-note pattern using each chromatic pitch once
the absence of a pitch that stands out as the home note.

MC-0283.name: Tritone
cues: a stark, tense pitch gap spanning three tones.

MC-0284.name: Turn
cues: a quick curl around one note: above–main–below–main
the inverted version starting below.

MC-0285.name: Hemiola
cues: beat accents regrouping from two groups of three into three groups of two, or the reverse
an apparent shift in the pulse without the notes slowing down.

MC-0286.name: Answer
cues: the fugue’s opening tune entering in a new part at a different pitch
an entry a fifth higher or fourth lower.

MC-0287.name: Antiphonal
cues: two groups taking turns and answering each other across the texture.

MC-0288.name: Bridge
cues: a linking passage moving from one main theme towards another
a shift into a new key during the linking passage.

MC-0289.name: Countersubject
cues: a recurring second tune accompanying the fugue’s main theme
the second tune continuing in the part that has just finished its entry.

MC-0290.name: Fugue
cues: one clear theme beginning alone
other parts joining with the same idea at different pitches
independent lines continuing to weave beneath later entries.

MC-0291.name: Inversion
cues: a tune’s upward steps becoming downward ones, and vice versa
the chord’s third in the bass for first inversion, or its fifth for second inversion.

MC-0292.name: Leitmotif
cues: a recognisable musical idea returning with the same character or dramatic situation
changes in its sound as the story develops.

MC-0293.name: Retrograde
cues: a tune or rhythmic pattern running backwards, last note first.

MC-0294.name: Song cycle
cues: a sequence of songs linked by words, mood or story
one singer with piano throughout.

MC-0295.name: Stretto
cues: a new theme entry beginning before the previous one ends
overlapping entries crowding together and building intensity.

MC-0296.name: Subject
cues: a distinctive main tune that returns or is developed.

MC-0297.name: Consort
cues: several sizes of one instrument family blending, often viols or recorders
contrasting families, such as strings and wind, mixed in a broken consort.

MC-0298.name: Countertenor
cues: male singing in an alto-like range
a light, clear, falsetto-like colour.

MC-0299.name: Piano trio
cues: piano, violin and cello clearly audible together
the tune and accompaniment passing between the three.

MC-0300.name: Sprechgesang
cues: a dramatic vocal line halfway between talking and singing
inflected pitches rather than notes held as a regular sung tune.
